After editing by hand, run: python3 tools/build.py. Or open the site with ?edit while tools/serve.py is running and use the editor.

work.title: Tesla
work.subtitle: Controls engineering intern
work.desc: Summer 2026 on the controls team at Giga Texas. I wrote Siemens PLC and HMI software, built a local AI and knowledge toolkit for controls work, and traced electrical faults on production lines to root cause.
work.summary: A summer as a controls engineering intern at Giga Texas. I worked on PLC and HMI software for production equipment and on a local AI and knowledge toolkit for controls work. On the line, my electrical root-cause work started from the drawings.

highlights.title: PLC and HMI applications
highlights.text: I developed and commissioned Siemens TIA Portal applications in SCL, ladder and function block diagram, on S7-1500 standard and fail-safe CPUs. That included the HMI tag models and operator workflows for production equipment.

highlights.title: Reusable interfaces
highlights.text: I built reusable PLC and HMI interfaces for dock-side indication, safety reintegration acknowledge paths, process interlocks and multi-axis debounce timing. Each one was checked online with watch tables before I handed it off.

highlights.title: Badge and RFID sign-in
highlights.text: I worked on badge and RFID sign-in for the production HMIs: normalizing credentials, handling the REST requests and responses, covering the SSO and tap-login paths, and fixing tags, scripts and endpoints that didn't match.

highlights.title: Reading the old binaries
highlights.text: I reverse-engineered legacy authentication helper binaries into readable control flow and mapped the identity chain against the Siemens project structure. I also built a Control Center integration for this site without carrying over another plant's configuration.

highlights.title: Interface specifications
highlights.text: I wrote PLC-HMI interface specifications that keep direct writes apart from cyclic abstraction layers, and put together an inventory of the plant's HMI and IPC addresses across several production lines.

highlights.title: A local model
highlights.text: I set up a local inference workflow over a private controls corpus, for SCL and HMI authoring and procedure routing.

highlights.title: A second brain for controls work
highlights.text: The knowledge base was structured Markdown with wikilinks and frontmatter metadata. The graph rebuilt itself and linked assets, blocks, faults and procedures, so I could follow a question several links deep.

highlights.title: Skills written as contracts
highlights.text: I wrote the agent skills as versioned Markdown contracts. Each one listed its preconditions, inputs, steps, acceptance checks and failure modes. They covered tracing a schematic, proving out a watch table, auditing HMI tag paths and filing a post-incident report.

highlights.title: Starting from the drawings
highlights.text: I traced power distribution, industrial network segments and safety circuits through the electrical schematics and panel drawings, and checked the hardware against the drawing package instead of guessing from the software alone.

highlights.title: Test cells
highlights.text: I wired and commissioned multi-device test cells with a PLC, remote I/O, an HMI, a pendant dock and a safety gate lock. On those cells I separated power and data cabling faults from application logic, and wrote up for the team how to tell them apart.

highlights.title: Intermittent faults
highlights.text: I led the isolation of intermittent faults on major production lines. I lined up bench baselines, PLC diagnostic buffers and the cable, switch and power paths from the schematics, and turned down raising watchdogs or timeouts as the fix.

highlights.title: Pendants that recover
highlights.text: I restored safety reintegration on the handheld operator pendants after a power loss, so an HMI acknowledge brings them back without a full PLC download. The causes were acknowledge tags that weren't bound and post-safety logic left out of the cyclic call tree.

highlights.title: Torque, debounce and an interlock
highlights.text: I fixed torque-limit selection so the at-speed limits latch after acceleration. I also put one HMI-adjustable debounce across several axes, and staged a cross-program process interlock that stays disabled until its setpoints pass safety validation.

work.title: 4D Mapping
work.subtitle: Object detection and AI optimization
work.desc: A computer-vision workbench I built. Give it an ordinary 2D video and it finds the objects, tracks them, and rebuilds the scene in 4D: x, y and z, plus time.
work.summary: A plain 2D video goes in. Object detection finds the subject in every frame, depth models and camera solving lift each frame into 3D, and the frames join up into one scene you can orbit and scrub through time. Earlier positions stay behind as ghosts, so you see the deer's whole path through the woods at once. The demo on this page came out of my own pipeline from a single clip. No 3D scanner, no extra cameras.

highlights.title: Space and time from one video
highlights.text: One ordinary video is enough. The pipeline solves the camera's path, tracks the subject frame by frame and places the whole scene in x, y, z and time.

highlights.title: Detection, measured
highlights.text: On a 1,000-image hold-out set, RF-DETR large finds people at 0.878 AP@0.50 in 35 ms a frame on an M5 Max. The small model that runs on the device gets 0.489.

highlights.title: What the stock detectors miss
highlights.text: Stock detectors miss subjects like a deer. For those, open-vocabulary detection and segmentation (Grounding DINO and SAM) find them and cut them out.

highlights.title: The photoreal version
highlights.text: There is also a photoreal version: Gaussian splats and per-frame 3D Gaussians, trained on the real frames and scored on frames held back from training.

highlights.title: Runs on its own
highlights.text: Drop a clip in a folder and the pipeline runs end to end and writes its own report.

highlights.title: Its own app
highlights.text: It has its own native desktop app, written in Rust on wgpu, with a 4D timeline, orbit, top-down and follow cameras, and a way to correct detections by hand.

work.title: ThinkFree Finance
work.subtitle: Founder and software engineer
work.desc: An AI platform I founded that turns financial news and public records into plain-English explanations, with the numbers checked against their sources.
work.summary: ThinkFree Finance explains markets for people who don't follow them for a living: renters, hourly workers, small-business owners, students. It reads the news, links it to public records and writes plain-English reports. A language model can state a wrong number as confidently as a right one, so the pipeline checks what it can and labels what it can't.

highlights.title: The news pipeline
highlights.text: News is collected, clustered by embeddings and summarized by a language model, with FAISS retrieval over economic reference texts. It's built to handle more than 1,000 articles a day.

highlights.title: Following the money
highlights.text: It connects politicians, bills, lobbying, congressional trades and public spending, using SEC EDGAR, OpenFEC, USASpending, BLS, Census and other public sources.

highlights.title: Checking the numbers
highlights.text: Numbers in a generated report are checked against the source data. If a summary fails the check, it's held back.

highlights.title: Website and app
highlights.text: A FastAPI website with accounts, MFA, CSRF protection, role-based access and a hash-chained audit log, plus a SwiftUI iPhone app.

highlights.title: My own security review
highlights.text: In October 2026 I did my own security review. Every bug I found is logged with the test that proves it's fixed.

work.title: hardcaml-pwm
work.subtitle: Digital hardware design in OCaml
work.desc: A rotary-encoder knob that sets a PWM duty cycle, written in Jane Street's Hardcaml. The duty glides to each new value instead of jumping.
work.summary: A small piece of digital hardware, written in OCaml with Jane Street's Hardcaml. Turn a rotary encoder and the PWM output follows, sliding to the new duty cycle over a few periods instead of jumping there. It's simulated and tested, and the Verilog is generated. It's still a learning project, though, and hasn't run on an FPGA board yet.

highlights.title: A PWM that glides
highlights.text: Each new duty-cycle target ramps in over a fixed number of periods and lands exactly, with no rounding error.

highlights.title: Reading the encoder
highlights.text: A quadrature decoder for an EC11-style rotary encoder: synchronizers, debouncing, direction from the A and B edges, and a click only on a real detent.

highlights.title: Tested in simulation
highlights.text: Every block has waveform tests in simulation, and the Verilog comes straight out of the OCaml.
